680.title: Pray for one another (James 5:13–20)
680.hook: sick? call the elders; suffering? pray; cheerful? sing
680.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians celebrate the anointing of the sick as a sacrament based in part on James 5:14–15, and many Protestant churches have elders or ministers anoint and pray over the sick; most churches also pray for the sick by name in worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the patient farmer, and Job, whose patience argued and still held on. Your line was be patient.

Some letters end with a long goodbye. James doesn't. No greetings, no names, no farewell. His last paragraph reads like a list on the fridge before a long trip: if this happens, do this. Sad? Happy? Sick? Wandering? There's an instruction for each. And almost every one points to the same thing. Not a technique, not a rule. Other people, and prayer. The last word of a blunt, practical letter is about how a community holds each other up.

In the King James Bible: "Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms." Every mood has a place to go: hard days, bring them to God; good days, sing. Then: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." Notice who moves. The sick person calls, and the elders come to the bedside. Oil was a common medicine in the ancient world, and also a sign of being set apart for God. Churches practice this verse differently. For Catholic and Orthodox Christians, it's one of the roots of a sacrament, the anointing of the sick. Many Protestant churches also anoint and pray over the sick, as a practice of prayer rather than a sacrament. Then: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much." One to another: not only up to God, but sideways, to each other. And James's example is encouraging. Elijah, he says, was a man subject to like passions as we are. An ordinary human, moody, tired, frightened at times. He prayed, and rain was held back; he prayed again, and it came. You don't need to be a giant; ordinary people's prayers matter. The very last line: whoever brings back someone who has wandered from the truth saves a soul and covers a multitude of sins. The letter ends not with a farewell, but with someone going after someone else.

Think of someone who is ill right now, a friend, a parent, a child, someone you've only heard about, and picture where they are and what they might be feeling. If you pray, pray for them by name in your own words, one for another, as James says; if you don't, hold them in your attention with care and wish them well.
Elders. The ones the sick are told to call in James's last instructions: come to the bedside, pray, anoint with oil, and hold each other up.
Your line: going after someone who wandered. That's where James chooses to end his letter. Six hundred eighty days, and counting.

681.title: What we have touched (1 John 1:1–4)
681.hook: the elder writes of what he has seen, heard and touched
681.howItsDone: Some churches read 1 John 1:1–4 in the Christmas season, as a witness that the Word became flesh, and use the letter's opening when teaching about fellowship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of James, and the elders called to the bedside. Your line was going after someone who wandered.

You can read a whole biography of someone, dates, places, letters, photographs, and still not know the feel of their handshake, or how their voice sounded saying a name. Some knowing goes through the eyes and ears, and some goes through the skin. Today a new letter opens, called First John. It has no greeting, no name, no to-whom. It starts mid-breath, like a witness on the stand who can't wait to say what he knows. And the first thing he talks about is touch.

In the King James Bible: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life." The senses pile up. Heard. Seen. Looked upon, a word for gazing, taking it in. And then, handled: the word means to feel for something, the way you reach out in the dark. From the beginning echoes the first line of John's Gospel: in the beginning was the Word. For this writer, the Word of life is someone you could touch. Who's writing? The letter never says. Tradition says John the apostle, and the style is close to John's Gospel. Some scholars think it comes from a community shaped by that Gospel, and hear the same voice as the one who calls himself the elder in Second and Third John. Either way, he speaks as a witness: we were there, we saw, we touched. Why say it this way? Because some people, it seems, were teaching that Jesus only seemed to have a real body, a spirit wearing a costume. The writer answers with his own hands: we touched him; he was real flesh. Then the purpose: "That which we have seen and heard declare we unto you, that ye also may have fellowship with us." Fellowship is a deep word: sharing, partnership, a common life. Not a club. And the reason he's writing at all: "And these things write we unto you, that your joy may be full." Not to win an argument. So the joy can be full.

Put your hand on something near you, the table, a cup, your own arm, and feel its temperature, texture and weight; you don't have to believe it's there, you know it through your hand. Then let your mind move to one person whose hand you've held, and remember the feel of it. If you pray, give thanks for what is real and near.
Fellowship. First John's reason for writing at all, a deep word for sharing, partnership, a common life: so that your joy may be full.
Your line: joy made full. This letter begins with touch. That's day six hundred eighty-one.

682.title: God is light (1 John 1:5–10)
682.hook: if we confess, he is faithful to forgive
682.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess sins to God in the presence of a priest in the sacrament of confession; some Protestant services include a spoken prayer of confession, sometimes introduced with 1 John 1:8–9, followed by words of forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the opening of First John, and fellowship, a shared and common life. Your line was joy made full.

Walk into a dark room and flip on the light. The first thing you see is not the furniture. It's the mess: the clothes on the chair, the dust on the shelf, the mug you forgot. In the dark, the room seemed fine. In the light, it's honest. That's why some of us prefer dim lighting. Today's passage starts with a statement about God that is three words long in English, and then moves straight to what happens to our mess when that light comes on.

In the King James Bible: "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all." No shadows in the corners, nothing half-true. Then the conclusion: if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another. Light is also about honesty between people. Then a run of ifs, like doors. If we say we have fellowship with God while walking in darkness, we lie. And: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." The danger isn't having a mess; the letter takes for granted that there is one. The danger is saying there isn't. Then the open door: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." The Greek word for confess is built from same and say: to say the same thing, to agree. To confess is to finally say about your life what God already says about it, what the light already shows. And the response isn't a lecture. It's faithful and just. Faithful, because God keeps his promise to forgive. Just, because the letter has just said that the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin. Churches practice confession differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess to God in the presence of a priest, in the sacrament of confession or reconciliation. Many Protestants confess privately to God, or together in a prayer of confession during worship, and some confess to a trusted friend.
screen: `CONFESS: SAY THE SAME AS THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Picture a lamp coming on in a room inside you, and let it shine on one thing you've done, or not done, that you've been avoiding. Name it plainly, without excuses and without beating yourself up, saying the same thing the light says. If you pray, say it to God and rest in the words faithful and just to forgive; if you don't, sit a moment in the relief of not pretending.
Confession. Saying the same thing about your life that the light already shows, and finding God faithful to forgive.
Your line: faithful to forgive. The light shows the mess, and the door stays open. Rest well.

683.title: The old new commandment (1 John 2:1–11)
683.hook: whoever hates his brother walks in darkness
683.howItsDone: Christians remember the new commandment especially on Maundy Thursday, whose name is usually traced to the Latin mandatum, commandment, and many churches read 1 John 2 when teaching about love within the community.

segments.voice: Yesterday: God is light, and confession, saying the same thing the light shows. Your line was faithful to forgive.

Is it old or new? The writer of First John can't seem to decide, and that's the point. Within two verses he says, I'm not writing you a new commandment, it's an old one. Then, right away: actually, it is new. It sounds like a man changing his mind mid-sentence. It isn't. Ask a couple married for decades: the same words, I love you, can be very old and brand new at once. Today, the commandment that is both.

He starts tenderly: "My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous." An advocate stands beside you in court and speaks for you. Then a simple test: how do we know we know God? We keep his commandments, not just say we do. Then the riddle: "Brethren, I write no new commandment unto you, but an old commandment which ye had from the beginning." Which old commandment? Love. It runs back through the Torah: "love thy neighbour as thyself," in Leviticus. It's what his readers heard from the very beginning of their faith. Then he flips it: "Again, a new commandment I write unto you." New, because in John's Gospel, at the Last Supper, Jesus says, "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another." New, because now it has a face: love as he loved. And new, the writer says, "because the darkness is past, and the true light now shineth." It's dawn: something old seen in fresh light. Then the hard edge: "He that saith he is in the light, and hateth his brother, is in darkness even until now." Whoever hates walks in darkness and doesn't know where he's going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes. Hatred doesn't only hurt the other person; it takes away your own sight. Love is how you see where you're going.
screen: then, large: `THE TRUE LIGHT NOW SHINETH.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you hold something against, a small irritation or an old hurt, and notice what happens in your chest as you picture them. Ask quietly what this grudge has kept you from seeing, about them, about you, about the way forward, without trying to fix it now. If you pray, pray for them by name.
Advocate. First John's name for Christ with the Father: someone who stands beside you in court and speaks for you when you sin.
Your line: walk in the light. An old command, in a new dawn. Day six hundred eighty-three, done.

684.title: Little children (1 John 2:12–17)
684.hook: the elder writes tenderly to children, young people and elders
684.howItsDone: Some churches read 1 John 2:12–14 as a blessing for every age in a congregation, and the warning about the lust of the eyes and the pride of life comes up in teaching on simple living.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the old new commandment, and Christ as advocate, speaking for us. Your line was walk in the light.

Families have pet names. Kiddo. Sweetheart. Buddy. Some grandparents call grown adults by a childhood nickname to the end, and nobody minds, because it isn't about age. It's about belonging. The writer of First John has a pet name for his readers, and he keeps coming back to it: little children. Today he stops the flow of the letter for a little poem, short lines to everyone in the room, young and old, and then a warning about what can pull them away.

In the King James Bible: "I write unto you, little children, because your sins are forgiven you for his name's sake. I write unto you, fathers, because ye have known him that is from the beginning. I write unto you, young men, because ye have overcome the wicked one." Then he goes round the circle again. Little children: you're forgiven. Fathers, the older ones: you have known him a long time. Young people: you are strong, the word of God lives in you, and you've already won a battle. Scholars aren't sure whether he means actual ages, stages of faith, or all three said to everyone at once. On that last reading, every reader is a little child who is forgiven, a mature one who knows, and a young one who is strong. Notice what he doesn't do: scold. Every line turns on because: because you're forgiven, because you know, because you've overcome. He writes from what's already true of them. Then the warning: "Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world." That can sound strange next to John's Gospel, where God so loved the world. But world here seems to mean something else: the way of life that leaves God out. He names it: "the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life." Wanting, looking, showing off. Appetite, envy, status. Then perspective: "And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever." Trends pass. The one who does the will of God abides.
screen: then, large: `I WRITE UNTO YOU, LITTLE CHILDREN.`

If you pray, pray for each by name.
Little children. The writer's pet name for his readers: forgiven, belonging, written to because of what's already true.
Your line: the world passeth away. His pet name says you belong. See you tomorrow.

685.title: What manner of love (1 John 3:1–3)
685.hook: see what love: that we should be called children of God
685.howItsDone: Many Christians read 1 John 3:1–2 at baptisms and on All Saints' Day, and the line about seeing God as he is shapes Christian hope in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant teaching alike.

segments.voice: Yesterday: little children, the writer's pet name, and lines written from what's already true. Your line was the world passeth away.

Somewhere in a lot of families there's a box: crayon drawings, a first shoe, a report card, a lock of hair. Plenty of people only find it as adults, clearing out a closet, and it stops them cold: someone kept all of this, because it was mine. A love they never saw, kept the whole time. Today's passage is three verses long, and it begins with that kind of surprise. The writer has been talking about light and darkness, sin and commandments. Then he stops, as if overcome, and says: look.

In the King James Bible: "Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God." Behold: look at this. What manner of love: the Greek phrase carries surprise, something like, what kind of love is this? Bestowed is a gift word. Not earned. Given. And the gift is a name: called children of God. A detail from the manuscripts: the oldest Greek manuscripts add three more words, and so we are. Called children of God, and so we are. The manuscripts behind the King James didn't have them, and modern translations usually put them back. It's as if the writer worried someone would think called was only a title. It's what you are. Then why the world doesn't always see it: "therefore the world knoweth us not, because it knew him not." If people missed who Jesus was, they'll miss his children too. Then the future, and what he admits he doesn't know: "Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be." Already, but not yet finished. What he does know is that when he appears, "we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is." And the last verse says hope like that changes how you live now: whoever has this hope purifies himself.
screen: `BEHOLD: WHAT KIND OF LOVE IS THIS?`
`NOW, BUT NOT YET WHAT WE SHALL BE.`
`WE SHALL SEE HIM AS HE IS.`

segments.voice: Notice the names you call yourself in a hard moment, failure, too much, not enough, without arguing with them. Then set beside them the name the letter uses, children of God, with your own name in front of it if you pray, or a plainer one if that phrase isn't yours: I am loved. Rest there, and just look.
Bestowed. First John's gift word, not earned, but given: the Father's love that lets us be called children of God, and so we are.
Your line: children of god. Called, and so we are. That's day six hundred eighty-five.

686.title: In deed and in truth (1 John 3:11–18)
686.hook: love not in word only but in deed
686.howItsDone: Christians organizing meal trains, collections and visiting sometimes quote 1 John 3:18, and churches read it alongside James 2 on faith and works.

segments.voice: Yesterday: what manner of love, bestowed as a gift, not earned. Your line was children of god.

A heart emoji takes half a second. A sympathy post takes ten. Driving across town with soup takes an afternoon. All three can be sincere, but only one is warm when it arrives. For days now, First John has circled love: old, new, the love that names believers children of God. Today he gets very practical. He reaches back to Cain and Abel, then asks a question about a bank account and a neighbor in need. A letter that can sometimes float comes down to earth.

In the King James Bible: "For this is the message that ye heard from the beginning, that we should love one another." Then the counterexample, from the first pages of Genesis: don't be like Cain, who killed his brother. Whoever hates his brother, the writer says, is a murderer at heart. Hatred is the seed; Cain shows what it grows into. So what does love look like? Not a feeling first. A shape. "Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren." For Christians, the cross is the measure of love. Then, right away, the writer brings it from the heroic to the everyday. Laying down a life is rare. But: "whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?" Bowels of compassion sounds odd to us. The Greek word means the inner organs, the gut, where feeling was felt. We still say a gut feeling. The picture is someone who sees a need, feels that tug inside, and shuts it off. Then the line the passage builds to: "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth." In deed: something done. In truth: something real, not a performance. That closes a week from the end of James into First John: pray for one another, what we have touched, God is light, the old new commandment, little children, what manner of love, and in deed and in truth.
